tasks.title: Study for Science Quiz (Periodic Table, EMS, & Percent Abundance) - Ms. Dube
tasks.emailBody:
Hello,

Thank you for your information.

The notes are simplified in order to help all students understand chemistry. Your explanation would support a course that is more in-depth.

I would be more than happy if you would like to present your knowledge to the chemistry class! Please let me know if, when and what topic you would like to share about. It is always neat to have others share their knowledge as it could spark something for another student.

Blessings,

Ms. Dube

[cid:c8a5c61e-a291-4858-b83b-9f9a29e766ce]
________________________________
From: Eric Smith 
Sent: Tuesday, September 15, 2026 9:06 PM
To: Crystal Dube 
Subject: Re: Ben's notes

Hi, I was just reviewing these with Ben and noticed some mistakes:

General observation (not a mistake): you appear to be focusing on electromagnetic waves. My PhD was actually in multiphase fluid dynamics and wave stability between gasses and liquids — different waves, similar concept. Point being, the applicability of what you’re teaching extends beyond electromagnetics into fluids, sound, vibrations, etc. Cool for the students to realize the broad applicability of what they’re learning.

Anyway, mistake 1: (point 8) Frequency is not wavelength divided by time. We can see by dimensional analysis this would give us units of speed (distance/time) and frequency is in Hz or 1/s or 1/time. I think you wanted ’n/t’ (number of waves per time) or if you wanted to include wavelength you need to use f = v/λ (velocity/wavelength) which also gives you 1/time.

Mistake 2 (or confusingly worded): on point 7, a wavelength is not necessarily ‘midpoint to midpoint’ because that would give you half a wavelength. I’m sure you meant the midpoint to midpoint with a matching slope, but as stated it might be confusing for a student.

Clarifications: These are items I felt missed some specificity. I tried rewording to see if they might be helpful in your teaching...

 * Number 2: NRP might be easier to understand as 'the point where the wave's amplitude goes to zero’ or even easier: 'the midpoint between the trough and the crest' (a stationary or standing wave has no velocity so where’s the NRP?)
 * Number 10, perhaps you want to say “the maximum speed a wave can travel is the speed of light, which is how fast electromagnetic waves travel in a vacuum.” ‘c' is the speed limit of the universe!
 * Number 12: Wavelengths for visible light are often measured in nanometers (no other waves that I can think of are in this range)

Hope this helps and I’m glad they’ll be getting practice with unit conversions here.

Eric

On Sep 15, 2026, at 7:54 PM, Crystal Dube wrote:

Hello,

I hope your week is going well.

Attached are the notes for Ben from being absent. If I missed one, please let me know. I am still working on Blackbaud.

The topics for the quiz are:

Knowing how to read the PTE; Mendeleev & Mosely; Know the order of EMS based on the wavelength/frequency (an image of the scale will be there); patterns/trends of PTE; know the family names & relation to valence electrons; stay familiar with Bohr, Rutherford, Thomson; know how to calculate percent abundance.

Please let me know if you have any questions.

Thanks,

Ms. Dube

tasks.title: AP World History Unit 1 Test (Ashley Johnson)
tasks.emailSubject: Westlake Lutheran Academy: Benjamin Smith - Classroom Reminder
tasks.emailBody:
Student Name: Benjamin Smith 
 Author Name: Ashley Johnson 
 
 Comment Date: 09/10/2026 
 Comment Type: Classroom Reminder 
 Comment: Dear Parents and Students,

Our AP World History Unit 1 Test will be Thursday, September 17. Students have several resources available to help them prepare. I strongly encourage students to begin reviewing early rather than waiting until the night before the test.
Unit 1 Study GuideThe Unit 1 Study Guide is a graded assignment and is due on the day of the test, Thursday, September 17. Students should use the study guide to review the major developments, concepts, and vocabulary from Unit 1.
AP World Unit 1 Study Guide
Blooket ReviewStudents can use the Blooket to practice Unit 1 content and check their understanding. I recommend completing the study guide first and then using the Blooket for additional practice.
AP World Unit 1 Blooket Review
Heimler's History Unit 1 Review VideosHeimler's History is an excellent resource for reviewing AP World History Unit 1: The Global Tapestry. Students should begin with the complete Unit 1 review video and then use the individual topic videos to review areas where they need additional practice.
Heimler's Unit 1 Review Video

Students do not need to rewatch every video in the playlist. Instead, they should focus on topics they are less confident with.
Heimler's Complete Unit 1 Video Playlist

Recommended Study Plan: Complete the study guide → practice with the Blooket → watch Heimler's Unit 1 review → use individual Heimler videos to strengthen weaker topics.

Because this is an AP course, students should make sure they understand not only important people, places, and vocabulary, but also the larger historical developments, connections, and comparisons from Unit 1.

Please encourage students to take advantage of these resources throughout the week. Students are also welcome to ask questions in class if there are Unit 1 topics they would like us to review again before the test.

Thank you for your support!
Mrs. Johnson
